name: Herbal teas, ginger, lime and spices for colds and flu
what_people_do: Drink hot infusions, decoctions and "punch" made from local herbs (mint family especially), often with ginger, lime or honey, at the first sign of a cold; Haitian families did this in the COVID period.
why_they_say_it_works: Heat, sweating and the plant itself are believed to "break" the cold.

documented_by.source: Thesnor V et al 2024, PMID 39273867 (TRAMIL-style survey, Haiti)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: 120 Haitians interviewed with the TRAMIL questionnaire: 75 plants from 43 families for COVID-19, influenza and respiratory illness; Lamiaceae the commonest family; infusion, decoction and punch the usual methods.

documented_by.source: Homemade plant-based foods and beverages as community responses to COVID-19 (rapid survey incl. Jamaica), 2020, J Ethnobiol Ethnomed, PMID 33298108
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Rapid survey (Jamaica among 17 case studies): people relied mainly on teas and spices, repurposing everyday homemade remedies for flu.

documented_by.source: Clement YN et al 2015, J Ethnobiol Ethnomed, PMID 26369926 (TRAMIL survey, Trinidad)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Trinidad: Leonotis nepetifolia was the plant reaching 20% citation for cough and common cold.

4 users describe family remedies for colds and coughs: (1) an Afro-Barbadian user, black tea with lime and rum for a cold or sore throat; (2) hot water with lemon, honey, garlic, ginger, cayenne and cinnamon for congestion; (3) crushed garlic in warm milk with honey; (4) chewing cloves for a cough. Only the first states a Caribbean origin; the others do not state a region. Forum evidence documents use only; the tier is unchanged.

evidence.finding: Fewer colds on garlic supplement (24 vs 65), but "insufficient clinical trial evidence"; claims rely largely on poor-quality evidence.

source.name: Garlic for the common cold, Cochrane 2014, PMID 25386977

evidence.tested: Honey for acute cough in children
evidence.finding: Honey probably reduces cough frequency vs no treatment or placebo (moderate certainty).

source.name: Honey for acute cough in children, Cochrane 2018, PMID 29633783

evidence.tested: Steam (heated humidified air) for the common cold
evidence.finding: Uncertain whether it relieves symptoms; fixed and random-effects analyses disagree.

source.name: Heated, humidified air for the common cold, Cochrane 2017, PMID 28849871

evidence.tested: The Caribbean herbs themselves (Leonotis, Lamiaceae teas)
evidence.finding: No human trial retrieved for the plants actually cited. Thesnor's authors say many are "scientifically validated" but name Samyda rosea as unresearched; I did not check the validation claim.

source.name: agent4-traditional-practices.md, 12 Nov 2026 (research file in this project)

harm_note: Hot drinks are low risk; the harm is delay when a child or older person has breathing difficulty (general advice, not from these sources).
gaps: No source opened tests hot water and lime specifically.
Honey is not safe under 12 months (general guidance, not in the Cochrane abstract read).
Tier D is for the herbs cited; honey and garlic are separate lines.
